slides.sub: You may listen privately, and stop at any time
slides.title: Room 9: Conflict Itself
slides.narration: Welcome to Lesson 14, the last room. This lesson is about disagreement itself. You may listen privately, and you may stop at any time.

slides.quote: “Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger, and give no opportunity to the devil.”
slides.narration:
Let’s begin with Scripture. Ephesians chapter 4, verses 26 and 27.

“Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger, and give no opportunity to the devil.”

slides.title: Not about marriage as such
body: Paul writes to believers about how they live together as one body. It speaks to anyone who lives closely with other people, including a husband and a wife.
slides.narration: Paul is writing to believers about how they live together as one body. This is not a passage about marriage as such. But it speaks to anyone who lives closely with other people, and that includes a husband and a wife.

slides.kicker: Notice what he does not say
slides.title: “Be angry and do not sin”
body: Not “never be angry.” Anger quickly becomes an occasion for sinful words, actions and settled resentment.
slides.narration: Notice what Paul does not say. He does not say, “Never be angry.” He says, “Be angry and do not sin.” Anger is not automatically sin, but it quickly becomes an occasion for sinful words, actions and settled resentment. Paul’s concern is both what we do in anger and whether we allow it to remain.

slides.title: Do not let the sun go down on your anger
body: Urgency about not nursing anger, not a rule to stay up all night. Some conversations need a break. Anger should not be carried and stored.
slides.narration:
Then he gives a direction: “Do not let the sun go down on your anger.” Take that as urgency about not nursing anger, not as a rule that you must stay up all night until everything is settled. Some conversations need a break, and we will come to that. The point is that anger should not be carried and stored.

And he gives the reason: “Give no opportunity to the devil.” Anger that is fed and stored can create an opportunity for further harm.

slides.title: Danger lies in unaddressed anger
body: Truth, self-control, repentance, forgiveness and timely repair keep a marriage from being governed by whoever is angriest.
slides.narration: That is the truth this lesson stands on. Anger is not automatically sin, but unaddressed anger, and what we do when we are angry, is where the danger lies. Truth, self-control, repentance, forgiveness and timely repair are what keep a marriage from being governed by whoever is angriest at the moment.

slides.title: Not a couple who never disagrees
body: A couple who knows how they disagree, what they will refuse to do to each other, and how they find their way back.
slides.narration: So the aim of this room is not a couple who never disagrees. It is a couple who knows how they disagree, what they will refuse to do to each other, and how they find their way back.

slides.title: Fewer arguments is not the measure
body: One couple argues often and repairs well. Another rarely argues because one stopped speaking honestly two years ago. The second may be in far more danger.
slides.narration: There is a second mistake to avoid. Some people define a good marriage as one with fewer arguments. But one couple argues often and repairs well. Another rarely argues because one of them stopped speaking honestly two years ago. The second couple looks better, and may be in far more danger. What matters is whether both people are free to speak, and what happens during and after a disagreement.

slides.title: Acting out the cycle they sat down to discuss
body: “Whenever we argue, you shut down.” “I shut down because you attack me.”
slides.narration:
Let me describe how this usually goes wrong, and then how to look at it differently.

The irony is that talking about how you fight often becomes a fight. One says, “Whenever we argue, you shut down.” The other says, “I shut down because you attack me.” The first says, “I only get sharp because you never listen.” Within a minute, they are acting out the exact cycle they sat down to discuss.

body: One raises something. The other becomes defensive. The first intensifies. The second withdraws. Both say, with total sincerity: “I only did that because you did the other thing first.”
slides.narration: In an ordinary disagreement, the pattern often looks like this. One person raises something. The other becomes defensive. The first becomes more intense. The second withdraws. The first pursues harder. The second shuts down. At the end, both can say with total sincerity, “I only did that because you did the other thing first.”

body: Pursue and withdraw, escalating together, or both avoiding. Roles may change by topic. Each of you remains responsible for your own actions.
slides.sub: Not “who is the problem?” but: what happens between us when something becomes emotionally difficult?
slides.narration:
Some couples fall into pursue and withdraw. Others escalate together, or both avoid the issue. Roles may change by topic. Describe your actual pattern rather than trying to fit a label. And notice that each of you remains responsible for your own actions, even when you can explain what you were reacting to.

So the question is not “Who is the problem?” It is: what happens between us when something becomes emotionally difficult?

slides.title: What usually starts a difficult conversation between us?
body: Take a moment before you go on.
slides.narration: Pause here. What usually starts a difficult conversation between us? Take a moment before you go on.

slides.kicker: What are you trying to protect?
body: One may be protecting themselves from feeling controlled, the other from feeling abandoned. This explains ordinary conflict. It does not excuse intimidation.
slides.narration: Here is a question that changes how you see it: what are each of you trying to protect when you disagree? One may be protecting themselves from feeling controlled. The other, from feeling abandoned. One is fighting for respect; the other, for safety. Understanding that can help explain ordinary conflict. It does not excuse intimidation, and it does not make one person responsible for the other’s harmful choices.

slides.note: Abuse is not a shared communication loop. Responsibility for abusive conduct belongs to the person using it. If disagreement makes you afraid, or one of you cannot refuse, raise a concern or speak honestly without punishment, do not use the language of “our cycle.” Stop the joint exercises and speak to someone outside the relationship.
slides.narration: Now a caution that matters. Everything I have just said is about ordinary conflict, between two people who can safely disagree. Abuse is not a shared communication loop. Responsibility for abusive conduct belongs to the person using it. If disagreement in your relationship makes you afraid, if one of you cannot refuse, raise a concern or speak honestly without punishment, do not use the language of “our cycle.” Stop the joint exercises and speak to someone outside the relationship.

list: How long do our unresolved conflicts stay unresolved?
Who usually moves first towards repair?
What tells us a difficult conversation is actually finished?
slides.narration: For everyone else, look at repair. How long do our unresolved conflicts stay unresolved? Who usually moves first towards repair? Is it usually the same person? If it is, you may have developed a pattern in which responsibility for repair falls unevenly. Name it before resentment grows. Can I say, “I was wrong”? Can I change my position after the conversation has started? And when a difficult conversation ends, what tells us it is actually finished? Couples often stop talking without resolving anything and treat the silence as resolution. You need a marker that means finished, something you say or do that both of you recognise.

slides.title: Who are we going to be when conflict comes?
body: That is not a technique. It is an identity, decided in advance, or by whoever is angriest.
slides.narration: Behind all of it is a larger question. Who are we going to be when conflict comes? That is not a technique. It is an identity, and it is decided in advance, or it is decided by whoever is angriest at the time.

slides.title: Three sentences, fifteen to twenty minutes
list: When I am hurt, my instinct is to…
What I need my spouse to remember about me during conflict is…
The person I want to become when we disagree is…
slides.narration: Your step has two parts. First, separately, about fifteen to twenty minutes. Each of you completes three sentences in writing. When I am hurt, my instinct is to… What I need my spouse to remember about me during conflict is… And, the person I want to become when we disagree is… The third is the important one. The first two describe who you are. The third describes who you are choosing to become, and it is the only one you have any control over.

slides.title: 45 to 60 minutes, in private
list: Exchange your sentences. Ask questions. Do not argue.
Describe what happens between you when something becomes difficult, without deciding who started it.
slides.narration: Then set aside 45 to 60 minutes, in a private place, when neither of you is tired. Have your Lesson 2 rules in front of you. Work through three main questions. First, exchange your sentences. Read them, and ask questions. Do not argue. Second, describe what happens between you when something becomes emotionally difficult, without trying to decide who started it. Third, write your Conflict Covenant. It is a statement of who you intend to be towards each other when it is hard.

list: We will not use conflict to punish each other.
We will not threaten to end the relationship as a tactic.
We will tell the truth before resentment becomes silence.
We will take a break when overwhelmed, and come back.
We will apologise without waiting for the other.
We will not demand agreement as proof of love.
slides.narration: Here is a starting set. Take what fits, change what does not, and add what only applies to the two of you. We will not use conflict to punish each other. We will not threaten to end the relationship as a tactic for frightening or winning against each other. Serious decisions about the relationship will be discussed calmly and may include wise outside support. We will tell the truth before resentment becomes silence. We will take a break when we are overwhelmed, we will agree when to return to the conversation, and we will come back. We will protect private information while remaining free to seek wise, confidential support. We will apologise without waiting for the other to apologise first. And we will not demand agreement as proof of love.

body: Five years from now, when we have a disagreement we cannot quickly solve, what do you want to be able to say about how I treated you?
slides.narration: Then close by answering one question out loud. Five years from now, when we have a disagreement we cannot quickly solve, what do you want to be able to say about how I treated you?

slides.kicker: The sentence you are building towards
body: “Even when we disagreed, you treated me with dignity, and I remained free to speak honestly.”
slides.narration: The sentence you are building towards is not, “We never had conflict.” It is, “Even when we disagreed, you treated me with dignity, and I remained free to speak honestly.”

slides.kicker: If you find a real disagreement
body: Do not panic, and do not minimise it. Do not solve it in one conversation. If it cannot be resolved before the wedding, do not hide it because the date is approaching.
slides.narration: If you find a real disagreement, do not panic, and do not minimise it. A serious disagreement does not automatically mean the engagement should end, but it may be a reason to pause. Do not solve it in one conversation. Understand it first. And if it cannot be resolved before the wedding, do not hide it because the date is approaching. A delayed wedding is far easier to manage than a deeply unresolved marriage.

body: “We have taken this as far as we can on our own.” Asking for help is not a sign that your relationship has failed.
slides.narration: Asking for help is not a sign that your relationship has failed. Sometimes the wisest sentence available is, “We have taken this as far as we can on our own.”

slides.title: Keep it going
body: Once a week or once a fortnight, twenty to thirty minutes. Begin with something you appreciated.
slides.narration: And when you marry, do not put all of this away like a textbook after an exam. Choose something ordinary and regular, once a week or once a fortnight, twenty to thirty minutes. Begin with something you appreciated. That keeps honesty from becoming something you only do when something has gone wrong.

body: Lord, thank You that You are patient with us. Teach us to be angry without sinning, and to bring what hurts into the light before it settles. Give us honest words, gentle hearts and the humility to say, “I was wrong.” Keep us in truth and in love. Make our home a place where each of us can speak and be heard. Amen.
slides.narration:
Let me close with a short prayer.

Lord, thank You that You are patient with us. Teach us to be angry without sinning, and to bring what hurts into the light before it settles. Give us honest words, gentle hearts and the humility to say, “I was wrong.” Keep us in truth and in love. Make our home a place where each of us can speak and be heard. Amen.

slides.title: Thank you
slides.sub: May the God of peace lead you in truth, love and faithfulness.
slides.narration: Thank you for walking through these rooms. May the God of peace lead you in truth, love and faithfulness.
